Keep all usage on demand, and rely on sustained use discounts to lower the cost until the migration is complete.

explanation: Compute flexible CUDs are spend-based. They apply to eligible spend on Compute Engine, GKE, and Cloud Run in any project and region of the Cloud Billing account. The deciding requirement is that the discount must stay in use while workloads move between services and regions. Size the commitment to the hourly spend that stays steady during the whole term.

whyWrong.A: A resource-based commitment covers only N2 resources in `us-central1`. As services move to GKE Autopilot, Cloud Run, and `europe-west1`, you still pay the commitment fee, but less usage consumes it.
whyWrong.B: Service-specific commitments for Cloud Run and for GKE Autopilot are no longer available for purchase. Google tells you to purchase compute flexible commitments instead.
whyWrong.D: Sustained use discounts apply only to Compute Engine and GKE VMs in some machine series, not to Cloud Run. They give less than a 3-year commitment and don't meet the finance goal.

sources.title: Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine
sources.evidence: With a compute flexible commitment, you can receive applicable CUDs on eligible Compute Engine spend across the commitment's Cloud Billing account, regardless of the project or region where you use your Compute Engine resources.

sources.title: Committed use discounts
sources.evidence: Cloud Run service-specific commitments are no longer available for purchase.

stem: A research lab links its projects to one Cloud Billing account. A team lead created an alerts-only budget of $2,000 per month for one project, with threshold rules at 50%, 90%, and 100%. The lead believes that the project stops when its spend reaches $2,000. What should you tell the lead?

options.text: At 100%, Cloud Billing pauses all billable services in the project until the next month starts.
The budget only sends alerts. Services keep running and keep accruing charges above $2,000.
At 100%, Cloud Billing disables billing on the project, and all of its resources stop.
At 100%, the Compute Engine quotas of the project drop to zero, so no new VMs can start.

explanation: An alerts-only budget sends notifications when actual or forecasted cost passes a threshold. It doesn't stop services or block billing. To act on spend, connect the budget to Pub/Sub and automate a response, or use a spend cap budget (Preview) for an eligible service.

whyWrong.A: Only a spend cap budget (Preview) pauses usage, and only for one eligible service in one project. An alerts-only budget never pauses services.
whyWrong.C: Cloud Billing doesn't disable billing by itself. You must build that response with Pub/Sub and a function, and Google warns that it can delete resources.
whyWrong.D: Budgets don't change quotas. Quotas are a separate control that doesn't react to spend.

sources.title: Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts
sources.evidence: they don't automatically prevent the use or billing of your services when the alerts-only budget amount or threshold rules are met or exceeded

sources.title: Manage spend cap budgets
sources.evidence: Spend caps are limited to budgets that are scoped to a single Google Cloud project and a single eligible service within the specified project.

stem: A company gives each data science team its own development project. The teams run Compute Engine VMs for experiments and keep the results in Cloud Storage. Management wants an automatic action when a development project exceeds its monthly budget. The action must stop further compute cost without any risk to the stored results. What should you do?

options.text: Connect each project budget to a Pub/Sub topic, and deploy a Cloud Run function that disables billing on the project when cost exceeds the budget.
Create a spend cap budget (Preview) for Compute Engine in each project, so that Compute Engine usage pauses at the budget amount.
Set the Compute Engine CPU quota of each project to a low value, and raise it again at the start of each month.
Connect each project budget to a Pub/Sub topic, and deploy a Cloud Run function that stops the running VMs when cost exceeds the budget.

explanation: Budget notifications on Pub/Sub can trigger a Cloud Run function that controls resources selectively. Google's example stops Compute Engine VMs and leaves the Cloud Storage data intact. The deciding requirement is to stop compute cost while the stored results stay safe.

whyWrong.A: Disabling billing shuts down all resources in the project, and resources might be deleted irretrievably. This puts the stored results at risk.
whyWrong.B: Compute Engine is not an eligible service for spend cap budgets (Preview), so you can't create this budget. Spend caps cover only the Gemini API, Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions. Spend caps also don't pause persistent resources, such as compute and storage services.
whyWrong.C: Quotas limit amounts of resources, not cost. A low CPU quota doesn't react to the budget, and it blocks work even when a team is under budget.

sources.title: Control resource usage with notifications
sources.evidence: If you need a more nuanced response, you can selectively control resources. For example, you can stop some Compute Engine resources while leaving Cloud Storage resources intact.

sources.title: Disable billing usage with notifications
sources.evidence: This tutorial removes Cloud Billing from your project, shutting down all resources. Resources might be irretrievably deleted.

sources.title: Manage spend cap budgets
sources.evidence: In this release, the eligible services include Gemini API, Agent Platform (formerly known as Vertex AI), Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions.

stem: A company has 30 product teams. Some teams share projects, and each team runs development and production resources. Finance wants a monthly showback report of cost by team and by environment. Analysts want to use SQL and to see which individual resources drive cost. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add team and environment labels to each project, and group the Cloud Billing reports by those label keys.
Create one budget for each team with a label filter, and collect the monthly totals from the budget alert emails.
Define a standard set of labels, such as team and environment, and enforce it on every resource through Terraform.
Enable the detailed usage cost export from Cloud Billing to a BigQuery dataset in a FinOps project.
Create one project for each team and environment, and move all shared resources into them before the next report.

explanation: Labels on resources flow into Cloud Billing data, so you can split cost by team and environment even inside a shared project. The detailed usage cost export to BigQuery adds resource-level cost and supports SQL analysis. The deciding requirements are shared projects, which make project-level data too coarse, and resource-level analysis in SQL.

whyWrong.A: A project label can't split a shared project between teams. Also, when you group Cloud Billing reports by label keys, you don't see labels that are applied to a project.
whyWrong.B: Budgets compare spend with a target and send alerts. They are not a reporting tool, and they give no resource-level data for SQL analysis.
whyWrong.E: Moving all shared resources into new projects is a large and risky change. It still gives no SQL analysis or resource-level detail.

sources.title: Labels overview
sources.evidence: Labels are exported to BigQuery with the corresponding Google Cloud resources and their usage.

sources.title: Export Cloud Billing data to BigQuery
sources.evidence: The detailed export schema includes everything in the standard usage cost data plus resource-level cost data, like a virtual machine or SSD that generates service usage.

sources.title: Analyze billing data and cost trends with Reports
sources.evidence: When grouping by label keys, you don't see labels that are applied to a project.

stem: A company creates a central FinOps team. The team must create and edit budgets for all projects and manage the export of cost data to BigQuery. The security policy says that the team must not link projects to billing accounts or change payment settings. Which role should you grant to follow the principle of least privilege?

options.text: Billing Account Costs Manager on the Cloud Billing account
Billing Account Administrator on the Cloud Billing account
Billing Account Viewer on the Cloud Billing account
Project Billing Manager on each project that the team supports

explanation: Billing Account Costs Manager can create, edit, and delete budgets, view cost information, and manage the export of cost data to BigQuery. It can't link or unlink projects or manage the properties of the billing account. The deciding requirement is least privilege with rights for budgets and exports.

whyWrong.B: Billing Account Administrator can also link projects, manage payment methods, and manage other users. That breaks the security policy.
whyWrong.C: Billing Account Viewer gives read access to cost information. It can't create budgets or manage the export.
whyWrong.D: Project Billing Manager links and unlinks projects, which the policy forbids. It doesn't manage budgets or exports.

sources.title: Cloud Billing access control and permissions
sources.evidence: Create, edit, and delete budgets, view billing account cost information and transactions, and manage the export of billing cost data to BigQuery.

sources.title: Cloud Billing access control and permissions
sources.evidence: Doesn't allow the linking or unlinking of projects or otherwise managing the properties of the billing account.

stem: A retailer runs BigQuery with on-demand pricing. Dashboards and scheduled reports create a steady query load all day, and the monthly query cost changes a lot from month to month. Finance wants a predictable monthly cost for this steady load and a discount for committing to it. What should you recommend?

options.text: Keep on-demand pricing, and set a project-level custom quota on the bytes that queries can process each day.
Create a Standard edition reservation with a baseline for the steady load, and buy a 3-year slot commitment for it.
Create an Enterprise edition reservation with a baseline for the steady load, and buy a slot commitment for that baseline.
Keep on-demand pricing, and partition and cluster the largest tables to reduce the bytes that each query scans.

explanation: Capacity pricing bills slot-hours, and baselines and commitments make the bill predictable. A slot commitment gives a discount for the baseline, and only the Enterprise and Enterprise Plus editions offer slot commitments. The deciding requirements are a predictable cost and a commitment discount.

whyWrong.A: A custom quota sets a daily limit on on-demand bytes. It limits spend by blocking queries, so dashboards can fail, and it gives no discount.
whyWrong.B: Standard edition has no access to capacity commitments, so you can't buy a slot commitment for it.
whyWrong.D: Partitioning and clustering reduce the bytes scanned, but on-demand cost still changes with usage. There is no commitment discount.

sources.title: Estimate and control costs
sources.evidence: Enterprise and Enterprise Plus editions also provide optional one- or three-year slot commitments that can save money over the pay-as-you-go rate.

sources.title: Introduction to workload management
sources.evidence: With capacity-based billing, you allocate processing capacity for workloads with the option of automatically scaling capacity up and down when needed.

sources.title: Understand BigQuery editions
sources.evidence: Capacity commitments are not required to purchase slots, but can reduce costs.

stem: A bank runs a business-critical fleet of N2 VMs in the `us-east4-a` zone. The fleet size has been stable for two years and will stay stable for three more. The bank must be sure that it can recreate the VMs in that zone after a failure, and it wants the lowest price for this usage. What should you recommend?

options.text: Purchase a 3-year compute flexible commitment that covers the hourly spend of the fleet.
Purchase a 3-year resource-based N2 commitment in `us-east4`, and attach a reservation for the VMs in `us-east4-a`.
Purchase a 3-year resource-based N2 commitment in `us-east4`, because the commitment holds capacity for the fleet.
Create a reservation for the VMs in `us-east4-a`, and keep the VMs on on-demand pricing without a commitment.

explanation: A resource-based commitment gives a discount for stable N2 usage in the region, but it doesn't reserve capacity. A reservation holds capacity in the zone. To get both a discounted price and reserved capacity, you purchase a commitment and create a reservation. You can attach the reservation to the commitment.

whyWrong.A: A flexible commitment gives a discount, but it reserves no capacity in the zone. The capacity requirement is not met.
whyWrong.C: A commitment is a price agreement only. It doesn't reserve capacity in a zone.
whyWrong.D: The reservation holds capacity, but on-demand pricing misses the discount that a 3-year commitment gives for stable usage.

sources.title: Resource-based committed use discounts
sources.evidence: A commitment provides a 1- or 3-year discounted price agreement, but it doesn't reserve capacity in a specific zone.

sources.title: Resource-based committed use discounts
sources.evidence: To get zonal resources at discounted prices and also makes sure that capacity is reserved for them, you must both purchase commitments and create reservations for those zonal resources.

stem: A media company runs two workloads on Compute Engine in one region. A nightly transcoding job uses 200 N2 VMs for about 6 hours, and the job retries failed segments. A web tier of 20 E2 VMs runs all day at a steady load and will stay for at least 3 years. The company wants to cut cost without changing the application architecture. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Purchase a 3-year compute flexible commitment sized to the hourly spend of the nightly transcoding fleet.
Run the transcoding VMs as Spot VMs, and let the job retry the segments of preempted VMs.
Keep the web tier on demand, because sustained use discounts reduce its cost automatically.
Purchase a 3-year resource-based N2 commitment for the 200 transcoding VMs.
Purchase a 3-year resource-based E2 commitment in the region for the web tier.

explanation: The transcoding job tolerates failure, so Spot VMs cut its cost: when VMs are preempted, the job slows but doesn't stop. The web tier has steady, predictable usage of one machine series in one region for 3 years, which fits a resource-based commitment. The deciding facts are the retry logic of the job and the steady usage of the web tier.

whyWrong.A: You pay the commitment fee every hour of the term, but the batch fleet runs only about 6 of 24 hours. Compute flexible commitments also don't apply to Spot VMs.
whyWrong.C: E2 is not one of the machine series that get sustained use discounts.
whyWrong.D: The N2 fleet runs about a quarter of each day. In Google's example, a commitment with a 30% discount needs more than 70% use in the month to break even.

sources.title: Spot VMs
sources.evidence: If your workloads are fault-tolerant and can withstand possible VM preemption, Spot VMs can reduce your Compute Engine costs significantly.

sources.title: Sustained use discounts
sources.evidence: Sustained use discounts apply only to the machine series listed in the Eligible resources and discount percentages section.

sources.title: Get recommendations for committed use discounts (CUDs)
sources.evidence: For example, if a commitment offers a 30% discount, then an instance needs to run for more than 70% of the month to break even.

stem: A company's analysts use BigQuery with on-demand pricing in one shared project. Last month, a few analysts ran very large exploratory queries that tripled the bill. The company wants a daily limit on the data that each analyst can process, so that one analyst can't use up a limit that the whole team shares. What should you configure?

options.text: A budget for the project with a 100% threshold rule and email alerts to the analysts
A reservation with a maximum number of slots, assigned to the project of the analysts
A custom quota on the bytes that the whole project can process each day
A custom quota on the bytes that each user can process each day in the project

explanation: BigQuery custom query quotas are proactive: a query that exceeds the quota doesn't run. The `QueryUsagePerUserPerDay` quota applies separately to each user and service account in the project. The deciding requirement is a daily limit for each analyst. Custom quotas are approximate: they are a safeguard against excessive spending, not a strict limit.

whyWrong.A: A budget only sends alerts. It doesn't stop any query.
whyWrong.B: Reservations belong to the capacity pricing model and limit slots, not bytes per analyst. The analysts use on-demand pricing.
whyWrong.C: A project-level quota is one total for all users. One analyst can use it up and block the whole team.

sources.title: Create custom query quotas
sources.evidence: Custom quota is proactive, so you can't run an 11 TB query if you have a 10 TB quota.

sources.title: Create custom query quotas
sources.evidence: QueryUsagePerUserPerDay: User-level custom quota is separately applied to all users and service accounts within a project.

sources.title: Create custom query quotas
sources.evidence: Custom quotas are approximate. The custom quotas feature provides an additional safeguard against excessive spending, but is not designed to strictly limit bytes processed.

stem: A manufacturer plans to move its data center workloads to Google Cloud. The CFO is used to hardware purchases that are depreciated over five years, and worries that cloud bills will be unpredictable. The workloads have a steady baseline all year and seasonal peaks in the fourth quarter. Which approach should you recommend to address the concern of the CFO and keep the elasticity of the cloud?

options.text: Cover the steady baseline with committed use discounts, run the peaks on demand with autoscaling, and set budgets with forecasted-cost alerts.
Size committed use discounts to the fourth-quarter peak, so that every hour of the year runs at the discounted rate.
Run all workloads on sole-tenant nodes, so that the finance team can classify the spend as capital expenditure.
Keep all usage on demand, and rely on sustained use discounts to lower and smooth the monthly bill.

explanation: In the cloud, most costs are OpEx and follow consumption. A commitment adds a fixed monthly fee for its term, which makes the baseline predictable at a lower price. On-demand autoscaling handles the peaks, and forecasted-cost alerts warn early. The deciding requirements are predictability and elasticity together.

whyWrong.B: You pay for a commitment for its full term, whether you use it or not. A commitment sized to the peak stays mostly unused for three quarters of the year.
whyWrong.C: Some services, such as sole-tenant nodes, might be classified as CapEx. But the concern of the CFO is predictability, and a change of accounting category doesn't make the bill predictable.
whyWrong.D: Sustained use discounts apply only to some machine series and change with usage. They don't make the bill predictable.

sources.title: Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar
sources.evidence: In the cloud, the costs for most cloud resources are treated as OpEx, where costs are incurred when the cloud resources are consumed.

sources.title: Committed use discounts
sources.evidence: This monthly fee applies to your purchased commitments for the entire duration of the commitment period.

stem:
A manufacturing company plans to move its data center to Google Cloud. Before the migration starts, the CIO wants to know how ready the organization is: how well teams learn new skills, how strongly leadership supports the move, how much of operations is automated, and how access is protected. The CIO also wants a target state and a way to find the gaps.

What should you use?

options.text: Migration Center, to discover the servers and to create a total cost of ownership report for the data center.
A Well-Architected Framework review of each workload, to score its reliability, security, and cost design.
Active Assist recommendations, to find idle resources and security risks in the current environment.
The Google Cloud Adoption Framework, to rate the Learn, Lead, Scale, and Secure themes on the Cloud Maturity Scale.

explanation: The CIO asks about organizational readiness in four areas: learning, leadership, automation, and security. These areas match the four themes of the Google Cloud Adoption Framework: Learn, Lead, Scale, and Secure. Google recommends that you evaluate the maturity of your organization before a migration starts. The framework maps where your IT capabilities are now and where you want to be, so it shows the gaps.

whyWrong.A: Migration Center discovers assets and estimates cost. It does not measure skills, leadership support, or other organizational readiness.
whyWrong.B: A Well-Architected Framework review checks the design of a workload against the pillars. It does not rate the maturity of the organization.
whyWrong.C: Active Assist gives recommendations for Google Cloud resources. It does not assess skills or leadership, and the company has not moved yet.

sources.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started
sources.evidence: The Google Cloud Adoption Framework serves both as a map for determining where your business information technology capabilities are now, and as a guide to where you want to be.

sources.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Get started
sources.evidence: Before starting your migration, you should evaluate the maturity of your organization in adopting cloud technologies.

sources.title: Google Cloud Adoption Framework
sources.evidence: To build a truly cloud-first organization, there are four realms you'll need to excel in, whatever your business goals. These themes will be the foundation of your cloud readiness.

stem:
An insurance company starts its first migration wave to Google Cloud. The architect must choose the team that migrates the first workload. The company wants the first move to build experience and patterns that later waves can reuse. It must not put the main line of business at risk.

Which team should the architect choose?

options.text: A motivated team with DevOps practices that owns a typical workload with few dependencies and has a sponsor with clear goals.
The team that runs the policy-pricing engine, because a success on the most critical workload convinces leadership fastest.
The team with the least cloud experience, because a first migration forces its members to learn Google Cloud quickly.
The team that owns an annual reporting tool that few people use, because a failure there affects almost nobody.

explanation: The first workloads let teams build knowledge and experience on Google Cloud, so the choice of first movers is crucial. Google recommends a highly motivated team that is eager to try Google Cloud, with business leadership that sets clear goals and sponsors the team. The workload should not be business critical, should be typical of the estate so that the patterns apply later, and should have few dependencies.

whyWrong.B: A mistake in the most critical workload can harm the main line of business, which the stem rules out.
whyWrong.C: An inexperienced team adds risk. Google recommends a motivated team with a history of modern practices for the first move.
whyWrong.D: Google says to avoid rarely used workloads. They add little momentum to the migration, and problems in them are hard to detect.

sources.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Assess and discover your workloads
sources.evidence: When choosing your first-movers, pay attention to the teams responsible for each workload. The team responsible for a first-mover should be highly motivated, and eager to try Google Cloud and its services.

sources.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Assess and discover your workloads
sources.evidence: if you choose a workload that's used only a few times per year by a low number of users, although it's a low risk migration, it doesn't increase the momentum of your migration

stem:
A logistics company plans to move its applications from VMware to GKE Autopilot and Cloud SQL within 9 months. The operations team knows VMware and on-premises databases well, but it has no Google Cloud experience. Leadership wants the internal team to run the new platform after the migration.

What should the architect recommend first?

options.text: Hire a partner to build and run the new platform with broad administrative access, and keep it as the first point of escalation.
Require every operations engineer to pass the Professional Cloud Architect exam before the team starts any migration work.
Compare the team's current skills with the skills that GKE Autopilot and Cloud SQL need, then train by role in sandbox projects.
Move the VMs to Compute Engine with the same design as VMware, so that the team can use its current skills without training.

explanation: The deciding requirement is that the internal team must run the new platform. Google recommends that you first assess the team: list the skills, the level of expertise for each skill, and the people who know most. The gap between these skills and the target managed services defines the training program. A free environment to test and learn is critical to the learning experience of the staff.

whyWrong.A: A partner with broad privileged access as the first point of escalation keeps the knowledge outside the company. This conflicts with the goal that the internal team runs the platform.
whyWrong.B: A certification for every engineer before any work delays the migration. It also does not target the gap between the current skills and GKE Autopilot and Cloud SQL.
whyWrong.D: This avoids the skills gap by dropping the target design. The stem sets GKE Autopilot and Cloud SQL as the target.

sources.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Optimize your environment
sources.evidence: You start by listing all skills, the level of expertise for each skill, and which team members are the most knowledgeable for each skill.

sources.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Optimize your environment
sources.evidence: For example, if you start using a managed service, you need the skills to provision, configure, and interact with that service.

sources.title: Migrate to Google Cloud: Assess and discover your workloads
sources.evidence: Creating a free environment for testing and learning is critical to the learning experience of your staff.

stem:
A bank's platform team built a shared deployment pipeline and monitoring stack on Google Cloud. After six months, only 3 of 40 application teams use it. The other teams say that their current tools work, and that a move takes weeks of rework for no clear gain. The CIO proposes a mandate: every team must move by the end of the quarter.

What should the architect recommend to increase adoption?

options.text: Make the move a small, mostly automated step, state the benefit for each team, and coach the teams while early adopters show results.
Support the mandate, and send every exception request to a change advisory board that meets once each month.
Send all developers to a week of training on the new platform, and then enforce the deadline of the mandate.
Move all 37 remaining teams in one planned weekend, and have the platform team do the rework for them.

explanation: The teams resist because the cost of the move is high and the benefit is not clear. Google SRE found that the cost of migration must be small relative to the net benefits of the new common solution. Otherwise, the migration itself blocks adoption. People also need time, coaching, and training. Incremental change with early wins helps the organization buy into the change.

whyWrong.B: A mandate with a heavyweight approval board does not lower the cost of the move, so the teams still see no gain. DORA recommends peer review instead of heavyweight change approval.
whyWrong.C: Training helps, but people also need time and coaching to close the gap between knowledge and ability. The weeks of rework also stay in place.
whyWrong.D: A single large move is the opposite of incremental change. It puts 37 teams at risk at the same time.

sources.title: Organizational Change Management in SRE
sources.evidence: We have learned that to achieve success, the cost of migration (from older, fragmented but specialized solutions) needs to be small relative to the net benefits of the new common solution.

sources.title: Organizational Change Management in SRE
sources.evidence: On the human side, in order to recognize and embrace change, people need time, coaching, and training in new tools and skills.

sources.title: Organizational Change Management in SRE
sources.evidence: An iterative approach can demonstrate early wins that help an organization buy into the vision of change and justify further investment.

stem:
At a retail company, architects keep reopening old design debates, such as why the checkout service uses regional GKE clusters. The reasons exist only in meeting notes and chat threads. New team members cannot find out why the team made each decision.

What should the architects do?

options.text: Create a change advisory board that must approve every future architecture change before teams implement it.
Write architecture decision records with the options, requirements, and decision reasons, and store them with the code in version control.
Publish a wiki page of the current architecture standards, and replace the old standards when the teams change them.
Record every design meeting on video, and store the recordings in a shared Cloud Storage bucket for new members.

explanation: An architecture decision record (ADR) captures the key options, the main requirements, and the decision itself. Readers can see why the team chose, for example, regional GKE clusters. Teams often store ADRs in Markdown close to the code. When a decision changes, the ADR keeps the previous decision and the reason for the change. This history helps new members and stops repeat discussions.

whyWrong.A: An approval board controls future changes, but it does not record why the team made past decisions.
whyWrong.C: A list of the current standards drops the options, the reasons, and the history, so the debates continue.
whyWrong.D: Recordings are hard to search, and they do not give a short, structured reason for each decision.

sources.title: Architecture decision records overview
sources.evidence: An ADR captures the key options available, the main requirements that drive a decision, and the design decisions themselves.

sources.title: Architecture decision records overview
sources.evidence: The ADR can help teams avoid a repeat of the same discussion points, and it can help provide historical context when teams revisit topics.

stem:
At a media company, the product team wants to release the streaming app every week. The SRE team wants to stop releases for a month after each outage. Each month, the two teams escalate the dispute to a vice president, who decides based on the latest incident. The CTO wants a repeatable and objective way to decide when releases go ahead.

What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Create a change advisory board with the SRE lead and the product lead, and have it approve each weekly release.
Set an availability target of 100% for the app, and stop releases whenever any user request fails.
Keep the final decision with the vice president, and send the VP a monthly report of incidents and releases.
Have both teams agree on an SLO and an error budget, and release only while error budget remains.

explanation: The deciding need is a repeatable, objective rule instead of a monthly escalation. In Google SRE practice, the two teams define an error budget from the SLO. The budget is an objective metric for how unreliable the service can be in the period, and it removes the politics from the negotiation. Releases continue while error budget remains, and they stop or slow down when the budget runs out.

whyWrong.A: A board still decides each release by negotiation. It adds heavyweight approval but gives no objective rule.
whyWrong.B: A 100% target is probably never the right reliability target. It leaves no error budget, so releases would stop almost all the time.
whyWrong.C: The decision stays political and depends on the latest incident, which is the problem that the CTO wants to fix.

sources.title: Embracing Risk (Site Reliability Engineering)
sources.evidence: This metric removes the politics from negotiations between the SREs and the product developers when deciding how much risk to allow.

sources.title: Embracing Risk (Site Reliability Engineering)
sources.evidence: As long as the uptime measured is above the SLO—in other words, as long as there is error budget remaining—new releases can be pushed.

sources.title: Embracing Risk (Site Reliability Engineering)

stem:
A software company migrated its customer portal to Google Cloud. All services meet their SLOs, and infrastructure costs fell. However, the business sponsor calls the project a failure. The sponsor expected the move to let teams release features much faster, and release speed did not change. Nobody measured release speed during the project. The company now starts a second phase.

What should the architect do to make sure that the business can judge the second phase a success?

options.text: Tighten the SLOs of the portal services, so that the reports show the sponsor a higher level of reliability.
Buy Premium Support, so that a Technical Account Manager runs Operational Health Reviews of support and spend trends.
Agree with the sponsor on measurable goals for release speed, such as DORA software delivery metrics, and review them together regularly.
Hold a blameless retrospective of the first phase, and share the lessons learned with all the engineering teams.

explanation: The first phase met its technical targets but not the business objective, because nobody defined or measured that objective. Google recommends a measurable goal for each requirement. For faster and safer releases, DORA's software delivery metrics track the speed, ease, and safety of changes. Regular reviews with the sponsor use this feedback to steer the work.

whyWrong.A: Stricter SLOs measure reliability, which already meets its targets. They do not measure release speed, which is the sponsor's goal.
whyWrong.B: Operational Health Reviews cover progress, support, and spend with Google. They do not define or measure the sponsor's release-speed goal.
whyWrong.D: A retrospective helps the team learn from the first phase. It does not set a measurable goal that the sponsor agrees to for the second phase.

sources.title: Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework
sources.evidence: Using DORA's software delivery metrics can help your team monitor the speed, ease, and safety of making changes to the system.

stem:
A CIO wants to move a regional bank's workloads to Google Cloud. The CFO doubts the savings, and the head of compliance worries about the regulators. Two business unit leaders want different results: one wants lower costs, and the other wants faster product launches. The CIO asks the architect to prepare the adoption plan.

Which two actions should the architect take first? (Choose two.)

options.text: Write a vision statement of the business objectives and drivers, and get sign-off from the leading stakeholders and sponsors.
Start with the most visible customer-facing application, so that the doubtful leaders see quick results.
Ask the CIO to choose between the two business unit goals alone, so that the plan has one clear objective.
Choose the target Google Cloud services and publish a reference architecture before the first stakeholder meeting.
Run a proof of concept with success criteria that the CFO and the compliance head agree on, and share the results.

explanation: The stakeholders have competing visions and doubts. Google recommends that you agree on the key business and technical objectives and drivers, and get stakeholder sign-off, as the base for planning. A proof of concept with agreed success criteria then builds stakeholder confidence, because it shows tangible benefits to leadership and technical teams.

whyWrong.B: A critical, visible workload as the first move puts the main line of business at risk. It also skips the agreement on objectives.
whyWrong.C: A decision by one person leaves the other stakeholders out. Google recommends sign-off from the stakeholders who lead and sponsor the initiative.
whyWrong.D: A design before the objectives are agreed ignores the stakeholders. The architecture must follow the business objectives.

sources.evidence: Agreeing on the key business and technical objectives and drivers, then obtaining relevant stakeholder sign-off can provide a foundation for the next steps in the planning process.
